title: Burial, cremation, direct cremation, memorial service, and final disposition language

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source afterward/bereavement/funeral-language synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no individual legal, financial, funeral, clinical, mental-health, or ritual advice.
limitations: Public sources support broad vocabulary and practical context only; they do not supply consented room texture.
This record must not become legal, estate, financial, funeral, clinical, mental-health, diagnosis, ritual, or crisis advice.
Local law, institutional policy, funeral-home/cemetery/crematory requirements, clinicians, mental-health professionals, guardians, tradition holders, and the person’s wishes govern actual decisions.

moment.plain_scene: Someone must choose or confirm what happens to the body: burial, cremation, direct cremation, green burial, body donation, repatriation, memorial service, no service, or another lawful and culturally governed disposition.
ordinary_language_queries: burial or cremation what does final disposition mean
do you have to have a funeral

content_layers.observation_text: Someone must choose or confirm what happens to the body: burial, cremation, direct cremation, green burial, body donation, repatriation, memorial service, no service, or another lawful and culturally governed disposition.
content_layers.source_synthesis: Public funeral sources describe burial, cremation, direct cremation, funeral directors, self-arranged funerals, and legal requirements in different jurisdictions. The record keeps disposition language as vocabulary and witnessed decision pressure.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: Final disposition is a brutal phrase for an intimate decision. The archive should preserve who had authority, what the dead person wanted, what money allowed, what tradition required, and what felt unbearable.

what_this_is_not: not a recommendation for burial, cremation, donation, green burial, repatriation, or no funeral
not a legal guide to final disposition
not a claim that any one option is more dignified
uncertainties: Disposition options and requirements vary by law, local infrastructure, religion, culture, family authority, cost, and cause-of-death investigation.
Some practices are restricted, tradition-governed, or not public.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should make the phrase findable, orient the reader to why the moment is common enough to name, and then stop before giving personal legal, financial, funeral, mental-health, clinical, or ritual advice.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner or researcher surface should collect who had authority, what words were used, what the setting required, what the family understood, where conflict or exclusion appeared, and which local/professional supports were involved.
language_notes: Do not treat grief as a stage, task, timetable, performance, or disorder unless a qualified diagnostic context exists.
Keep legal, funeral, financial, child, and ritual content jurisdiction- and authority-bound.
Preserve ordinary words the bereaved use, including euphemism, anger, numbness, absence, and administrative speech.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the afterward, funeral/disposition, administrative-burden, and grief-language layer. It requires domain review before any public surface uses it.

safety.cultural_sensitivity: medium_to_high_because funeral body grief and family authority are culture bound
